content: The organization will analyze your responses, and all responses will be kept confidential. Participants are asked to circle their response on a scale of 1 to 5, where 1 represents strongly disagree, 2 represents disagree, 3 represents neither agree nor disagree, 4 represents somewhat agree, and 5 represents strongly agree. A questionnaire was distributed to workshop participants to gather feedback for evaluating the workshop and identifying areas for improvement in future Ministry and WHO activities aimed at strengthening family planning services in Kenya. The questionnaire and its results are included in the annexes. A total of 26 completed questionnaires were received and analyzed. The analysis focused on nine questions related to the workshop, with participants providing responses on the same 1-to-5 scale. The topics covered in the questionnaire included: 1. Clarity of the training session's objectives. 2. Improved understanding of the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) Wheel. 3. The importance of the MEC Wheel as a tool for family planning service provision. 4. Comfort in using the MEC Wheel. 5. Whether participants intend to use the MEC Wheel in their workplace. 6. Adequacy of time allocated for discussion and questions. 7. Usefulness of the adapted MEC Wheel for providers who do not typically offer family planning services. 8. Whether the adaptation of the MEC Wheel has resulted in a tool better suited to Kenya's needs. 9. Adequacy of time to adapt the MEC Wheel to Kenya's family planning needs. The overall opinions of participants are illustrated in a graph, showing that all 26 respondents strongly agreed on the importance of the MEC Wheel as a tool for family planning service provision. Eighteen out of 26 respondents felt that the workshop objectives were clearly defined, and 19 out of 26 strongly agreed that the adaptation of the MEC Wheel had produced a tool better suited to Kenya's needs and that there was adequate time to adapt the wheel. No participants strongly disagreed or disagreed with any of the questions. The annexes also include detailed feedback and suggestions from group discussions. Key points include: Permanent methods like bilateral tubal ligation (BTL) and vasectomy should be emphasized, with footnotes referencing Ministry of Health (MOH) guidelines. Barrier methods, such as condoms, require more visible and attractive messaging. Emergency contraception should have a separate column for copper IUDs, with clear footnotes. Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) should be highlighted with clear criteria and messaging. Post-abortion care should be treated as a distinct condition, separate from sepsis. Medical conditions should be arranged alphabetically for easier access. Survivors of sexual and gender-based violence (S/GBV) should be addressed, with emergency contraception included as a key message. The color scheme of the MEC Wheel should use traffic light colors for clarity: red for Category 4 (danger), green for Categories 1 and 2, and amber for Category 3. The MEC Wheel should always include its jacket during dissemination. Fertility awareness methods should be included but not routinely emphasized. Additional recommendations from group discussions include: The inclusion of natural methods like coitus interruptus and safe days, especially for youth. The addition of conditions such as renal disease, anemia, alcoholism, drug abuse, and goiter. Improved availability of the Pocket MEC Wheel for individual use. User-friendly design and information placement on the MEC Wheel and its jacket. The need for a wall-sized MEC Wheel and a desktop flip chart for easier reference. Fieldwork reports highlighted the following: Strong integration and referral systems between family planning (FP) and other services, such as maternal and child health (MCH) and comprehensive care clinics (CCC). Limited availability of the MEC Wheel in some facilities, with some providers relying on FP guidelines or charts instead. Challenges such as small consultation rooms, staff shortages, and stockouts of certain FP commodities. The need for training on the MEC Wheel to be integrated with FP training. Recommendations for improving the MEC Wheel include increasing font size, making it more user-friendly, and ensuring all information is included on the inner pages of the jacket. Overall, the feedback emphasizes the importance of adapting the MEC Wheel to local needs, improving its usability, and ensuring its availability to healthcare providers.
